title: The Pale Smile Again
premise: Bram Okonkwo, a property surveyor who survives by staying unremarkable, takes a routine appraisal of Hollowmere House and discovers the property responds to being measured—rooms shift, doors multiply, and the house appraises its visitors in return. His overnight sleep recordings reveal a second voice answering questions in his own timbre, a founder's echo that has waited decades for a body to finish the founding ritual. As Bram unravels the founders' covenant, he learns the house sustains itself by trading one resident's identity for the town's prosperity, and the second voice is his own future self, already hollowed. In the end Bram completes the ritual backwards, unbinding the covenant by surrendering his memories of the house rather than his self, walking out with a blank week in his mind and a town that slowly forgets him too.
about_author: Theo Thornbury is the pen name of a former building inspector who spent eleven years cataloguing condemned structures across the American Midwest before turning to fiction. They write horror about places that keep records, and they still refuse to sleep in houses built before 1950.

chapters.title: Square Footage
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. A meticulous surveyor who has survived trauma by being forgettable takes the Hollowmere appraisal job for triple his usual fee. The house measures oddly: rooms that gain a foot when he isn't looking. Emotional beat: quiet unease masked by professional routine.

chapters.title: The Doors Count Back
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. He counts eleven doors at dusk and nine at dawn, though the floor plan swears ten. A neighbor, Mrs. Adeyemi, warns him that the founders 'took inventory of people, not property.' Emotional beat: the first crack in his professional detachment.

chapters.title: Overnight Recordings
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, interleaved with recording transcripts. He leaves a recorder running and hears a second voice—his own, slightly wrong—answering questions no one asked aloud. Emotional beat: terror of being observed by something wearing his voice.

chapters.title: What the Founders Kept
chapters.summary: Bram's POV with archival documents. In the county library he finds the founders' ledger: every fifty years the house 'appraises' a resident, and the town prospers on the difference. The last entry is dated fifty years ago, next week. Emotional beat: dread hardening into purpose.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Names Itself
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The voice in the night recordings begins asking questions of its own, and answers Bram's memories back to him with small, loving corrections. It claims to be him, finished. Emotional beat: identity begins to feel negotiable.

chapters.title: Mrs. Adeyemi's Debt
chapters.summary: Mrs. Adeyemi's POV. She reveals her father was the last appraised resident: the town remembers him as a benefactor, but she remembers a man who came home with someone else's gait. Emotional beat: grief and complicity; Bram learns the price is communal.

chapters.title: Rooms That Remember Him
chapters.summary: Bram's POV. The house starts furnishing rooms to match his childhood—his mother's kitchen, a hallway he burned in a dream. The second voice grows stronger in daylight. Emotional beat: the horror of being known completely by a predator.

chapters.title: The Covenant's Fine Print
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, with the ledger's final pages. The ritual can be completed or reversed, but reversal requires the resident to surrender what the house has already appraised: his memories of the house itself. Emotional beat: the price of survival made explicit.

chapters.title: Appraisal Night
chapters.summary: Alternating Bram and second-voice POV. On the fiftieth anniversary the house seals itself; the voice walks him through the founding ritual in reverse while the town's lights flicker in sympathy. Climax: Bram speaks the unbinding, choosing blankness over erasure. Emotional beat: terrified resolve.

chapters.title: Vacant Possession
chapters.summary: Bram's POV, fragmented. He wakes on the porch with a missing week, files a report on a house the county records no longer list. Mrs. Adeyemi greets him like a stranger, kindly. Emotional beat: hollow, quiet peace—the cost paid, the self intact but lighter.
